analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the 'non-interference' rule that bars the Health and Human Services Secretary from interfering in drug price negotiations under Medicare Part D, and would instead direct the Secretary to negotiate with drug manufacturers for lower prices, the way other federal buyers such as the VA do. It would also require the Secretary to report to Congress twice a year on how the negotiations are lowering drug prices. The bill never moved beyond being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of Medicare beneficiaries, who pay Part D drug costs out of pocket and through premiums. If the Secretary could negotiate lower prices the way other federal agencies do when buying in bulk, beneficiaries' out-of-pocket costs and the government's share of drug spending could fall. Taxpayers generally, since Medicare picks up much of the drug bill.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory 'non-interference' provision that prohibits the HHS Secretary from interfering with negotiations between drug manufacturers and pharmacies and Part D plan sponsors, or from setting a price structure for Part D drugs.

Grants the Secretary authority 'similar to that of other Federal entities that purchase prescription drugs in bulk' to negotiate contracts with manufacturers of covered Part D drugs, in order to ensure beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price.
Requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the negotiations and how they are achieving lower prices for Part D drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose Medicare Part D revenues would fall if the Secretary wins lower negotiated prices. Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, who currently sit at the center of the negotiation process, could see the government take over part of that role.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and pricing intermediaries

drawbacks.text: The Secretary is given negotiating authority similar to other federal bulk purchasers, but the bill does not authorize the government to set prices or require manufacturers to sell at any particular level, so some analysts argue direct negotiation without that leverage could yield smaller savings than supporters hope.

Replacing negotiations run by private plan sponsors and pharmacy benefit managers with government negotiation could reduce plans' flexibility to structure their own formularies and pricing, a change the industry and some policy analysts warn could disrupt how Part D plans operate.

Drug manufacturers contend that government negotiation amounts to price controls that could reduce revenue available for developing new medicines, a cost borne in the form of less investment in future drugs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is potentially lower drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers, using a tool other federal buyers already use. The main uncertainty is how much leverage the Secretary would actually have without authority to set prices, and the transition would shift work now done by private insurers and pharmacy benefit managers to the government. On balance, the bill is a straightforward attempt to lower Medicare drug costs, with its effectiveness hinging on execution.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced the Prescription Drug and Health Improvement Act of 2013 in the Senate on January 23, 2013, joined by Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced; that referral is the last action in its record.
The bill ended the 113th Congress with no committee consideration and no vote in either chamber.

Versions of the same idea — repealing the Part D non-interference clause to let the government negotiate drug prices — were repeatedly introduced in this era and repeatedly stalled in committee, never reaching a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept selling to Medicare Part D plans without any government-negotiated prices, and the private plans and pharmacy benefit managers kept their central role in the pricing process. Beneficiaries gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers kept un-negotiated Medicare prices

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to authorize the HHS Secretary to negotiate Medicare Part D drug prices.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of its two original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; never scheduled it for a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no further action on it, leaving it without a hearing or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their lobby
against.role: Industry opposing government negotiation of Medicare drug prices
against.what_they_did: Fought repeated proposals to repeal the Part D non-interference clause and let the government negotiate prices.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; the bill's sponsor and its two cosponsors were all Democrats, and the committee that buried it was led by a Democrat, with no Republican involvement recorded either way.

industries.note: The bill would let the HHS Secretary negotiate Medicare Part D prices directly, the way other federal bulk buyers do, cutting the prices manufacturers currently charge. Their loss would be beneficiaries' savings in premiums and out-of-pocket costs.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers
industries.note: These intermediaries currently handle price negotiations between drug makers and Part D plans. Government negotiation could take over part of that role and constrain plans' pricing structures, while plans would still manage formularies and administer the benefit.
